title: Club good

definition.text: A good that people can be kept from using, usually by charging them, but that one person's use does not reduce for others until it gets crowded.

facts.text: Examples include cinemas, cable television, software as a service, and gym, golf club or swimming pool memberships.
Serving one more user costs almost nothing, so club goods are often supplied by natural monopolies and are kept artificially scarce.
Providers exclude non-payers either to cover fixed costs, as nonprofits do, or to make a profit.
Controlling access nearly always causes a deadweight loss, such as the cost of tollbooths or digital rights management.
The European Union has been treated as a club good: its services can be withheld from non-members, while adding members to the Schengen Area does not make travel harder for existing ones.

related: Intellectual property as an exclusion mechanism

definition.text: The branch of economics, founded by James M. Buchanan in 1965, that studies how big a group sharing a good should be and how it should share the costs.

facts.text: Buchanan saw a gap between purely private and purely public goods: excludable goods shared by more people than a private good but fewer than a public one.
Each new member lowers the cost per head but adds congestion, so there is an optimal club size that gives members the most benefit.
Cornes and Sandler's conditions lead to two-part pricing: a fixed membership fee plus a charge per use.
Olson and Zeckhauser (1967) applied the theory to cost-sharing in NATO, asking whether some members were free riding.

title: Coase theorem

definition.text: The claim that when one party's activity harms or helps another, the two can bargain their way to an efficient outcome, whoever starts with the property rights, provided bargaining costs are low enough.

facts.text: If true, the theorem would let private individuals solve externality problems by themselves.
Coase developed it while thinking about radio stations interfering with each other: the station that gained more from broadcasting would pay the other not to interfere.
If fencing the farm is cheaper than fencing the cattle, bargaining should produce a fence around the farm whether the farmer or the rancher holds the rights.
In his 1960 paper Coase himself argued that real transaction costs are rarely low enough for efficient bargaining.
Imperfect information and poorly defined property rights can also block the bargain.
In Danish talks between waterworks and farmers, farmers used their information advantage to seek over-compensation and drag out talks, showing how sensitive the theorem is to transaction costs.
Behavioral economist Richard Thaler found that people care about fairness when bargaining over their own property, so they may reject efficient but unfair deals.

contested_note: Critics argue the theorem rarely applies in practice, and Duncan Kennedy argues that the starting allocation of rights always matters.
distinct_from: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem

title: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem

definition.text: The two separate claims inside the Coase theorem: that bargaining gives an efficient result, and that it gives the same result whoever starts with the rights.

facts.text: Coase did not set out a single formal theorem; others built the loose formulation from his work.
Later authors showed the invariance claim is not generally true, because who bears liability changes wealth, which in turn changes demand and prices.
Steven Cheung extended it in 1969: without transaction costs, contracts, markets and corrective taxes can all reach the same efficient result.

title: Coasean bargaining failures
article: Coase theorem#Criticisms of the applicability of the theorem

definition.text: The practical reasons why private bargaining over harms such as pollution often fails to reach the efficient outcome the Coase theorem predicts.

facts.text: The assignment problem: with a polluted river it is hard to tell which factories caused the harm and who was hurt, and victims tend to overstate their losses.
The holdout problem: when many people hold rights, the last one can demand more, so everyone has a reason to demand more and bargaining unravels.
When many parties benefit equally from a deal, each has a reason to free ride by withholding payment.
In twenty legal nuisance cases studied by Ward Farnsworth, no party tried Coasean bargaining, out of anger at the unfairness of having to bargain.

distinct_from: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem

definition.text: How far the supplier of a good can stop people who have not paid from using it.

facts.text: Economists describe every good by two traits: how excludable it is and how rival it is.
A cinema film is excludable: ushers check tickets, so non-payers cannot see it.
A lighthouse is non-excludable, because any ship at sea can use its light.
Paul Samuelson proposed the idea in 1954 as a yes-or-no trait; Elinor Ostrom in 1990 recast it as a scale from fully excludable to fully non-excludable.
Music, films and software are semi-excludable: they have a price, but piracy lets many non-payers use them.
Because producers cannot profit from goods people get free, non-excludable goods tend to be under-supplied without government help.
